Tangling in the watercress crossing — one birch-bark hull dragging a green curtain of it broadside across the channel, a second shoving through the trailing stems with both fae rowing chest-deep in leaf, a third vaulting clean over the mat on a gust, a fourth slipping through the gap the bark hull tore open; a single mayfly hangs watching, broad as a racing fae is tall.

Dropping nose-first off the twig weir — the leading walnut shell buried to its rim in white water, one fae flat along the keel, a second hull catching air behind it and landing hard to port, a third still at the lip with its grass line dragging, a fourth riding a detached oak leaf down the slick face like a brown raft; the oak leaf wider than three hulls together.

Heeling right over on a squall — one petal sail, scarlet, flattened until its acorn hull nearly kisses the surface, a fae leaning far out off the windward rail to save it, a second boat spilling its plum petal loose and flopping bare-masted, a third rowing hard and low through the tilting field; a snail on the near bank keeps pace and, implacably, draws ahead.

Spinning stern-first in the eddy below the grey pebble — one fae digging a reed paddle against the curl to bring the hazelnut hull round, a second boat threading the eddy's outer lip in marigold sail, a third shooting through on the fast tongue inside them, a fourth backed off hard waiting; the pebble stands over the whole field like a slate cliff-face.

Overtaking under the bank with a petal sail brushing the reeds — one copper-skinned bark hull sliding through a gap barely its own width, the fae at its twig mast bent low under the fronds, a second hull crowding it from the channel side in berry-red, a third holding the racing line ahead blissfully unaware, a fourth closing fast behind with marigold sail cracked full; a reed stem rises taller than any mast in the field.

Lashed together shooting the narrow chute — two hazelnut shells bound at the gunwales with grass cord and rammed through side-by-side in a crash of white spray, the binding parting at the bottom and both hulls surging apart in opposite arcs, a third squeezing the gap a heartbeat behind them, a fourth already through and pulling clear into the sunlit pool; tucked under one thwart, a bronze-backed beetle rides the whole thing out perfectly still.

A duckling's wake rolling through the middle of the field — one bark hull lifted clean over the crest and coming down running with its cream petal sail cracking like a struck leaf, two acorn caps bailing furiously in the trough behind it, a third boat capsized and its fae riders hauling the grass lines to right it, a fourth skidding sideways across the top of the second wave; a floating oak leaf drifts past, broad as the three bailing boats laid end to end.

Bailing emergency at full speed — one moss-green shell riding low with a fae scooping water over the side stroke by stroke using an acorn cap in each hand, a second hull coming up fast on its windward quarter in deep plum sail, a third cutting inside it through the shallows, a fourth watching from behind with its oars raised to read the gap; the boot-shaped seed-pod hull sheds a thin silver arc of water with every fling.

A blown-petal squall blinding the leaders — a sudden gust of wild-cherry petals, white and cream, plastering across three petal sails at once and blinding the fae behind them, one hull swinging broadside in confusion, a second tucking its nose down and driving blind by feel alone, a third rowing bare-masted straight through the cloud into clear water with a full lead; one pink petal has lodged against a mast, unnoticed, fluttering there unnoticed the whole way down.

Mid-race repair on the move — one hazelnut hull going down by the bow while a fae slaps bark patch and pine resin over the split with flat bare hands, a second boat threading past on the port side in scarlet petal sail, a third bumping its hull against the stricken one to help and then thinking better of it and pulling away, a fourth already round the bend; a bulrush rises at the outside of the turn, taller than every mast in the field combined.

Two hulls grinding round the inside of the bend — one berry-red bark hull and one copper acorn hull locked beam-to-beam, their fae riders pushing off each other with feet braced on the opposite gunwale, neither giving a thumb's width, a third boat slipping the outside arc in marigold sail with water piling under its bow, a fourth tucking under the bank behind it; the turn is marked by a single rowanberry on a grass thread, bobbing in the churn.

A hull built too tall rolling clean over on the first crossing current — the tall birch-bark shell toppling slowly and then all at once, its fae flinging themselves onto the upturned keel, a second boat swerving wide around the wreck in cream petal sail, a third cutting inside the gap left open, a fourth stopping momentarily to stare and losing three boat-lengths to the decision; the hull lies bottom-up, and tied beneath its thwart a walnut-shell bailer still full of stolen water.

A paddle snapped clean in the eddy — one fae rowing on with a broad sycamore seed-wing held two-fisted, taking half-strokes in frantic circles to hold line, a second hull gliding past in plum sail with its fae wearing the expression of someone trying not to laugh, a third coming from behind fast in scarlet, a fourth jostling for the gap the broken stroke opened; the sycamore wing flexes with every pull and threatens to fold completely.

Racing bare-masted after a gust stripped the sail — one hazelnut hull driving on oars alone after its marigold petal sail is carried thirty lengths downstream, a second boat sheeting home a new sail, a moth wing with its amber eyespot showing, hung from a fresh twig mast at full speed, a third pulling clear in the lead, a fourth tangled in the fallen sail and dragging it like a cloak; the moth-wing sail trembles in the air and holds.

The tow going wrong — a grass line binding two hulls together snaps, the forward boat leaping ahead in a sudden surge of plum sail, the towed hull lurching back and spinning sideways into the path of a third, which swerves so hard its fae slides to the outer rail, a fourth cutting between all three with an opportunist grin; the snapped line coils on the surface a moment, then the current takes it.

Launching from the bank in a ragged shove — three hulls shoved into the stream almost together, one already crabbing sideways in the current, one straight and rowing hard in scarlet petal sail, one tangled in a reed stem with a fae pushing off it with both boots, a fourth already ten lengths ahead from an earlier start and looking back with clear satisfaction; the reed stem is as thick as that fae is tall.

Dead level in the last stretch — two shell hulls clicking oars together stroke for stroke under a marigold sail and a plum sail, a third driving under the bank with its sail let flat out in cream, its hull hidden in shadow, a fourth limping behind with a moss patch on its bow and losing ground it cannot get back; knotted to one bow, a clover head left from the last wreath ceremony drags a thin green wake.

Shooting through the twig gate neck and neck — two birch-bark hulls going through the bent-twig arch side by side with their oars overlapping in the gap, a fae on each boat pulling the crossed oar free mid-stroke, a third hull ramming the arch from behind and carrying the whole twig gate away on its bow, a fourth lifting its oars clear to wait; the arch leaves a bright green smear of lichen across the winning bow.

Capsized on the bend and hauling back — three fae knee-deep in the current righting their walnut hull on its grass lines, one already inside it bailing with an acorn cap while the others still push, a second boat swerving so wide around them it clips the far bank, a third shooting through the inside of the gap in deep scarlet sail, a fourth coming on hard behind; a water-vole watches from a root hollow, nose going, wholly unbothered.

A stowaway shifting the balance — the lightest hull in the field, a single curled birch-bark sliver, pulling clear of everything in plum sail while its fae looks puzzled by the speed, the five heavier boats working hard behind in the shade, a second hull edging close enough to see what is wrong, a third closing from the bank side; under the stern thwart a broad-backed river beetle rides out the whole race in perfect stillness.

A reed sweeping the leading mast clean — the front hull losing its twig mast and cream petal sail to a low-hanging frond in one silent swipe, both spinning end over end into the water ahead of the boat, the fae catching the mast stub and staring at it, a second hull threading between the wreckage and the bank in marigold, a third taking the mast clean in the chest and being knocked back into a fourth hull coming up hard; the fern frond hangs over the channel like a green vaulted roof and nobody warned anyone.

Surfing the fallen leaf over the twig weir — the leading fae balanced upright on a broad, drifting sycamore leaf, its walnut hull nested in the leaf's curl, the whole assembly riding the slick face of a twig dam in a smooth curving rush, a second hull trying the same move and catching its bow on the twig lip, a third portaging around the end of the dam in furious haste, a fourth watching from upstream and biding its time; the sycamore leaf is wide as the whole channel to everyone watching.

A blown-grass line fouling three hulls at the bend — one long strand of parted grass cord wrapping itself round an acorn hull's twig oar, trailing back to catch a second boat's bow, the third boat piling in behind it and all three slewing together, the fae on each reaching for the cord in the same moment and finding the others already there, a fourth threading the chaos in berry-red sail with its fae flat on the thwart; the whole tangle revolves slowly on the current and refuses to simplify.

Overtaking through a shaft of light — one copper bark hull breaking out of the shadow into a brilliant fall of sun, its marigold sail flaring gold from grey to blinding in a single hull-length, two more boats still labouring in the shade behind a watercress bridge, a fourth coming from the shadow on the other side in plum sail, both reaching for the same bright water; a dragonfly hovers in the shaft, wide as the hull is long, wholly absorbed in its own business.

A walnut shell spun by the eddy and rowed round again — its fae digging both leaf-oars in desperate asymmetric strokes to bring the bow back downstream, a second hull passing it broadside-on in scarlet petal sail with a fae calling something the noise of the water covers completely, a third shooting past on the inside in cream, a fourth approaching the same eddy with visible apprehension and taking the long way round losing two lengths to caution; the walnut hull completes its full circle and emerges going slightly faster than before.
